mainTopic: How the 613 מצוות were summed up by later נביאים, how משה's harsh decrees were softened, and the start of רבי עקיבא's hopeful story about רומי
overview: This amud finishes רבי שמלאי's teaching about the 613 מצוות. The word תורה adds up to 611, and the two commandments we heard directly from ה׳ bring the total to 613. Then the גמרא shows how later leaders summed up the whole Torah in fewer and fewer principles. דוד used eleven traits from תהלים פרק ט״ו, and each trait is matched to a role model. ישעיהו used six traits, then מיכה three, then ישעיהו again two. Finally חבקוק used one: 'וצדיק באמונתו יחיה'. Along the way, the חכמים comfort רבן גמליאל: even one trait is enough. Next, רבי יוסי בר חנינא teaches that four harsh decrees of משה were softened by four later נביאים, and the hopeful readings of 'ואבדתם בגוים' answer רב's fear. The amud ends with the start of the story of רבי עקיבא laughing at the noise of רומי, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: How 611 plus two makes 613
steps.stepSummary: The word תורה equals 611. Add אנכי and לא יהיה לך, which we heard directly from 'ה, and you get 613.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'תורה' adds up to 611. These are the מצוות that משה taught us. The first two commandments, 'I am' and 'You shall have no other gods,' we heard straight from the mouth of 'ה. Together that makes 613.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer it began just before this point. It explains why the פסוק 'תורה צוה לנו משה' fits the number 613.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number value of the letters in תורה is 611, which counts the מצוות that came through משה. The two missing מצוות, אנכי and לא יהיה לך, came directly from 'ה at הר סיני and not through משה. That is how the total reaches exactly 613.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I am (the Lord your God)', the first of the עשרת הדברות
'You shall have no (other gods)', the second of the עשרת הדברות
From the mouth of the Almighty, meaning directly from 'ה

steps.whatToRemember: 611 מצוות came through משה (the value of the word תורה), and 2 came directly from 'ה. Together they make the 613 מצוות.

phrases.english: is six hundred and eleven,
phrases.notes: This finishes a question from just before: what do the letters of the word תורה add up to?

phrases.english: 'I am' and 'You shall have no',
we heard them from the mouth of the Almighty.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֵׁית מְאָה וְחַד סְרֵי הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised just before this section: what is the number value of the word תורה?
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How does the פסוק 'תורה צוה לנו משה' match the count of 613 מצוות?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: תורה equals 611, and the two מצוות heard directly from 'ה complete the 613.

steps.title: A memory aid for the list of נביאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a string of letters to help remember the order of the נביאים it is about to quote.
steps.simpleTranslation: A memory sign: ד-מ-ש-מ-ק, ס-ק.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא gives a short memory aid before it lists how different נביאים summed up the מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each letter hints at one of the people or teachings coming up next, starting with ד for דוד. It is not a new teaching. It helps the learner keep the coming list in order.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid, a sign to help remember a list
The letters of the memory aid, hinting at the coming list of נביאים

phrases.english: (A memory sign: D-M-Sh-M-K, S-K.)
phrases.notes: These letters help you remember the order of the נביאים coming up, starting with ד for דוד.

steps.triggerLanguage: סימן דמשמק סק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from counting the 613 to a new list showing how later leaders summed them up.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A memory aid for the coming list.

steps.title: דוד sums up the מצוות in eleven traits
steps.stepSummary: דוד המלך took all 613 מצוות and stood them on eleven core traits, listed in תהלים פרק ט״ו.
steps.simpleTranslation: דוד came and based all the מצוות on eleven, as it says in תהלים: 'A psalm of דוד. Lord, who may stay in Your tent? Who may live on Your holy mountain? One who walks wholeheartedly, does what is right, and speaks truth in his heart. He has no slander on his tongue, does no harm to his friend, and does not insult his relative. A low person is disgusting in his eyes, and he honors people who fear 'ה. He swears even to his own loss and does not go back on it. He does not lend money with interest, and does not take a bribe against an innocent person. Whoever does these things will never be shaken.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues רבי שמלאי's teaching. דוד המלך took the 613 מצוות and gathered them into eleven main traits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד points to a few core traits that hold the whole Torah together. The פסוק asks who will 'stay in 'ה's tent' and answers with a list of qualities. Counting them gives the number eleven, and the next steps explain them one by one.

keyTerms.meaning: He stood them up on, based them on (summed them up)
One who walks wholeheartedly, with complete sincerity
He does not spread slander or gossip

steps.confusionAlert: דוד is not cancelling any מצוות. He is pointing to eleven core traits that the whole Torah rests on.
steps.whyThisMatters: This opens the famous list of how נביאים summed up the Torah in fewer and fewer principles. The list ends with חבקוק's single principle, 'וצדיק באמונתו יחיה'.

phrases.aramaic: בָּא דָּוִד וְהֶעֱמִידָן עַל אַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה,
phrases.english: David came and based them on eleven,
as it is written: 'A psalm of David. Lord,
phrases.notes: תהלים 15. The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: who shall stay in Your tent?
Who shall dwell on Your holy mountain?
One who walks wholeheartedly, and does righteousness,
and speaks truth in his heart.
He has no slander on his tongue,
he does no evil to his fellow,
and he does not take up an insult against his relative.
In his eyes a vile person is despised,
and he honors those who fear the Lord;
he swears to his own harm and does not change it.
He does not give his money out with interest,
and he takes no bribe against the innocent.
One who does these shall never be shaken.'

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּא דָּוִד וְהֶעֱמִידָן עַל אַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After setting the total at 613, the גמרא begins showing how דוד summed them up into fewer principles.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד based the 613 מצוות on eleven core traits from תהלים פרק ט״ו.

steps.title: 'Walking wholeheartedly' means living like אברהם
steps.stepSummary: The first trait, הולך תמים, refers to someone who acts like אברהם, whom 'ה told to 'walk before Me and be wholehearted.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'One who walks wholeheartedly' means someone like אברהם, as the פסוק says to him: 'Walk before Me and be wholehearted.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now starts explaining the eleven traits one at a time. It begins with the first one, הולך תמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא connects the words of the פסוק in תהלים to a matching פסוק about אברהם in בראשית. Both use the words 'walk' and 'תמים'. So the trait describes a person who lives with the complete trust and sincerity of אברהם.

keyTerms.meaning: Walk before Me ('ה's command to אברהם)
This refers to אברהם, meaning a person who acts like him

phrases.english: 'One who walks wholeheartedly':
this is Abraham,
phrases.notes: He means someone who lives the way אברהם did.

phrases.english: as it is written: 'Walk before Me and be wholehearted.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הוֹלֵךְ תָּמִים זֶה אַבְרָהָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts explaining the first of the eleven traits that were just listed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The trait הולך תמים describes a person who acts like אברהם, based on בראשית 17:1.

steps.title: Works righteousness: like אבא חלקיהו
steps.stepSummary: The second trait, פועל צדק, is shown by a person like אבא חלקיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Works righteousness' means someone like אבא חלקיהו.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second trait in the פסוק and points to אבא חלקיהו as a living example of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the first trait, this one is explained through a real person instead of a definition. The well-known story is that אבא חלקיהו was a hired worker who would not stop working even to return a greeting, because his time belonged to his employer. 'Working righteously' means being completely honest in the work you do for others.

phrases.english: "Works righteousness"
Such as Abba Chilkiyahu.

steps.triggerLanguage: פּוֹעֵל צֶדֶק כְּגוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of eleven traits begun in step 4, moving from trait one to trait two.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פועל צדק is shown by the example of אבא חלקיהו.

steps.title: Speaks truth in his heart: like רב ספרא
steps.stepSummary: The third trait, דובר אמת בלבבו, is shown by a person like רב ספרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And speaks truth in his heart' means someone like רב ספרא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third trait by pointing to רב ספרא as the example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key words are 'in his heart': this is truth that was never even said out loud. In the well-known story, רב ספרא decided in his mind to accept a buyer's price but could not answer because he was saying קריאת שמע. When the buyer raised his offer, רב ספרא still sold at the first price, because that was the deal he had agreed to in his heart.

phrases.english: "And speaks truth in his heart"
Such as Rav Safra.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדוֹבֵר אֱמֶת בִּלְבָבוֹ כְּגוֹן רַב סָפְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the same list of traits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דובר אמת בלבבו is shown by the example of רב ספרא.

steps.title: No deceit on his tongue: like יעקב אבינו
steps.stepSummary: The fourth trait, לא רגל על לשונו, is shown by יעקב אבינו, who was afraid of looking like a deceiver to his father.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Who has no slander on his tongue' is like יעקב אבינו, as the פסוק says: 'Perhaps my father will feel me, and I will seem to him like a trickster.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the fourth trait by pointing to יעקב אבינו and backs it up with a פסוק from בראשית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the last two examples, here the גמרא brings a פסוק as proof. When רבקה told יעקב to dress up as עשו, his first reaction was fear of being seen as a deceiver. That shows he naturally kept away from tricky, dishonest speech.

keyTerms.meaning: Went about with his tongue: spreading slander or deceptive talk

phrases.english: "Who has no slander upon his tongue"
phrases.notes: Literally 'did not go about on his tongue': he doesn't use his speech to deceive or gossip.

phrases.english: This is our forefather Yaakov,
As it is written: "Perhaps my father will feel me,
And I will be in his eyes like a trickster."

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא רָגַל עַל לְשֹׁנוֹ זֶה יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list; this time the example is supported by a פסוק, like אברהם in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לא רגל על לשונו is shown by יעקב אבינו, proven from בראשית 27:12.

steps.title: Does no evil to his neighbor: not taking over another's trade
steps.stepSummary: The fifth trait, לא עשה לרעהו רעה, means not moving in on another person's line of work.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Nor does evil to his neighbor' means he did not go into his friend's trade and take away his business.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the fifth trait, this time with a type of behavior instead of a named person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Doing evil to your neighbor' could sound like open harm, but the גמרא reads it as something quieter: cutting into another person's livelihood by competing in his trade. A truly upright person avoids even this kind of hidden damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Went into, entered (a field or business)

phrases.english: "Nor does evil to his neighbor"
That he did not go into his fellow's trade.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא עָשָׂה לְרֵעֵהוּ רָעָה שֶׁלֹּא יָרַד לְאוּמָּנוּת חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list; it switches from a named role model to a description of behavior.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: לא עשה לרעהו רעה means not cutting into another person's trade or livelihood.

steps.title: The sixth trait: keeping relatives close
steps.stepSummary: The trait 'וחרפה לא נשא על קרבו' describes a person who keeps his relatives close.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Nor takes up reproach against his relative' means a person who brings his relatives close.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the sixth trait in the list. It describes a person who keeps his relatives close and does not push them away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק uses the word קרבו, and the גמרא reads it as מקרב, bringing close. Even if a relative is a source of embarrassment, this person does not distance him.

keyTerms.meaning: His relative or someone close to him

phrases.english: "Nor takes up reproach against his relative"
This is one who brings his relatives close.
phrases.notes: There's a wordplay here: קרבו in the פסוק sounds like מקרב, 'brings close.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחֶרְפָּה לֹא נָשָׂא עַל קְרֹבוֹ זֶה הַמְקָרֵב אֶת קְרוֹבָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the same list of traits from the פסוקים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sixth trait is keeping one's relatives close instead of pushing them away.

steps.title: The seventh trait: despising the wicked, like חזקיהו
steps.stepSummary: The trait 'נבזה בעיניו נמאס' is shown by חזקיהו המלך, who dragged his wicked father's bones on a bed of ropes.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'In whose eyes a vile person is despised' is like King חזקיהו, who dragged his father's bones on a bed of ropes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives חזקיהו המלך as the example of the seventh trait. He did not honor his wicked father's body, even though it was his own father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person with this trait looks down on someone who is wicked, even a close family member. Instead of giving his father a royal funeral, חזקיהו dragged his bones on a simple bed of ropes, which was a public sign of disgrace.

keyTerms.meaning: A bed made of ropes, a cheap stretcher

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 9. Keeping relatives close is the normal rule. Here the relative was wicked, so חזקיהו treated him with disgrace because of his wickedness.

phrases.english: "In whose eyes a vile person is despised"
This is King Hezekiah,
who dragged the bones of his father
phrases.notes: His father was אחז, a wicked king.

phrases.english: on a bed of ropes.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִבְזֶה בְּעֵינָיו נִמְאָס זֶה חִזְקִיָּהוּ הַמֶּלֶךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list. It gives a person as the example, like the earlier steps did.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seventh trait is despising the wicked, as חזקיהו did with his wicked father.

steps.title: The eighth trait: honoring Torah scholars, like יהושפט
steps.stepSummary: The trait 'ואת יראי ה׳ יכבד' is shown by יהושפט מלך יהודה, who stood up from his throne for every תלמיד חכם.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he honors those who fear ה׳' is like יהושפט king of Judah. When he saw a Torah scholar, he got up from his throne, hugged and kissed him, and called him 'My father, my father, my teacher, my teacher, my master, my master.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives יהושפט as the example of the eighth trait, honoring people who fear ה׳. Though he was a king, he showed great love and respect to Torah scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This trait is the opposite side of the trait in step 10. Just as one should look down on the wicked, one should honor the righteous. A king getting up from his throne for a scholar shows that Torah outranks royal honor.

phrases.english: "And he honors those who fear the Lord"
This is Jehoshaphat, king of Judah,
who, whenever he would see a Torah scholar,
would stand up from his throne
and hug him and kiss him
and call him
"My father, my father, my teacher, my teacher, my master, my master."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶת יִרְאֵי ה׳ יְכַבֵּד זֶה יְהוֹשָׁפָט מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same פסוק as step 10, moving from despising the wicked to honoring the righteous.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The eighth trait is honoring Torah scholars, as יהושפט did by standing up from his throne for them.

steps.title: The ninth trait: keeping a costly promise, like רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The trait 'נשבע להרע ולא ימיר' matches רבי יוחנן, who would say 'I will fast until I get home' and then keep his word.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He swears to his own harm and does not change' is like רבי יוחנן, who said: 'I will be fasting until I come to my house.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי יוחנן as the example of the ninth trait. He kept his word even when keeping it was hard for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said 'I will fast until I get home' as a polite way to avoid eating somewhere. He then really fasted until he got home. A person with this trait keeps his commitment even when it hurts him.

keyTerms.meaning: Swears to his own harm, makes a promise that will cost him
And does not change it, does not take it back

phrases.english: "He swears to his own harm and does not change"
This is like Rabbi Yoḥanan,
as Rabbi Yoḥanan would say:
I will be fasting
until I come to my house.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִשְׁבַּע לְהָרַע וְלֹא יָמִר כְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list. It uses רבי יוחנן's habit as the example.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ninth trait is keeping one's word even when it causes oneself discomfort, as רבי יוחנן did.

steps.title: Not lending with interest, even to a non-Jew
steps.stepSummary: The trait 'כספו לא נתן בנשך' means he avoids interest even from a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He does not give his money with interest' means even interest from a non-Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next trait of the פסוק: this person stays away from taking interest, even in a case where he could.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taking רבית from a fellow Jew is already forbidden to everyone, so that alone would not make someone special. The praise here is that he avoids it even with a גוי, going beyond what he has to do.

phrases.english: "He does not give his money with interest"
even interest from a non-Jew.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the letter ב in round brackets; the meaning is the same either way.

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּסְפּוֹ לֹא נָתַן בְּנֶשֶׁךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of traits from the פסוק, moving to the next phrase.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The praised person refuses to take interest even from a גוי.

steps.title: Not taking a bribe, like רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The trait 'ושחד על נקי לא לקח' is shown by רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he does not take a bribe against the innocent' is like רבי ישמעאל the son of רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next trait by pointing to a sage who lived it: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply not taking a bribe is basic law for every judge. By naming a great sage as the example, the גמרא signals a higher level of caution about anything that might sway a judge.

phrases.english: "And he does not take a bribe against the innocent"
such as Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשֹׁחַד עַל נָקִי לֹא לָקָח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues to the final trait in the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The trait of not taking a bribe is shown by רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.whatToRemember: This finishes the eleven traits of תהלים 15. Each one was matched to an example or to a stricter level of behavior.

steps.title: רבן גמליאל cries over the closing words of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל read 'עושה אלה לא ימוט' as requiring all the traits, so he cried.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written, 'One who does these will never fall.' When רבן גמליאל reached this פסוק he would cry. He said: only someone who does all of them will not fall. But someone who does just one of them will fall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells how רבן גמליאל cried at the end of the פסוק, because he understood that only someone with all eleven traits is safe. This sets up the חכמים' response in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל read 'these' as 'all of these together.' That reading makes the promise almost impossible to reach, which is why he cried. His reading is the target the חכמים will answer next.

phrases.english: It is written: "One who does these will never fall"
phrases.notes: תהלים 15:5, the last words of the same chapter.

phrases.english: When Rabban Gamliel would reach
this verse, he would cry.
He said: one who does all of them,
he is the one who will not fall.
But one who does just one of them will fall.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּשֶׁהָיָה רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל מַגִּיעַ לְמִקְרָא הַזֶּה הָיָה בּוֹכֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the list of traits is finished, the גמרא turns to the closing promise of the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבן גמליאל reads the promise as applying only to someone who keeps all the traits.

steps.title: The חכמים: the פסוק says 'these,' not 'all these'
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים reject רבן גמליאל's reading: the word 'all' is missing, so even one trait is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Is it written, 'One who does all these'? It is written, 'One who does these,' meaning even one of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים answer רבן גמליאל by looking closely at the exact words of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל's fear depended on reading 'all' into the פסוק. The חכמים point out that the word 'all' is not there. So the promise applies to someone who does even one of these traits.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it written? (a challenge to a reading)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: מִי כְּתִיב ״עֹשֵׂה כׇּל אֵלֶּה״?
phrases.english: They said to him: Is it written, "One who does all these"?
"One who does these" is written,
meaning even with just one of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: מִי כְּתִיב עֹשֵׂה כׇּל אֵלֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly rejects רבן גמליאל's understanding of the פסוק.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבן גמליאל's reading that all the traits are needed.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: He read the word 'all' into a פסוק that does not contain it.

steps.title: Proof from 'אל תטמאו בכל אלה'
steps.stepSummary: Even the words 'all these' in another פסוק must mean 'any one of these,' as the טומאה פסוק shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you do not say this, another פסוק is written: 'Do not become impure with all these.' Would you say there too that only someone who touches all of them becomes impure, but with just one of them he does not? Rather, doesn't it mean with any one of all these?
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים back up their reading by bringing a different פסוק that uses the words 'all these.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ויקרא, 'בכל אלה' cannot mean you are only impure after doing every one of the sins; one alone is enough. So even when 'all' is written, it can mean 'any one.' That makes the חכמים' reading of 'these' in תהלים even stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: For if you do not say this
One who touches or comes in contact with
Rather, is it not that...? (leading to the proven point)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think this proof needs 'all' to mean 'all.' The point is the opposite: even where 'all' is written, it means 'any one,' so where it isn't written, one is surely enough.

phrases.english: For if you do not say this,
another verse is written:
"Do not make yourselves impure with all these."

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם נָמֵי, הַנּוֹגֵעַ בְּכׇל אֵלֶּה – הוּא דְּמִטַּמֵּא,
phrases.english: There too, is it only one who touches all these who becomes impure,
but with just one of them, no?
Rather, doesn't it mean with any one of all these?

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאִי לָא תֵּימָא הָכִי, כְּתִיב קְרָא אַחֲרִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the חכמים' reading from step 16 with a parallel פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That 'עושה אלה' means even one of the traits.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ויקרא 18:24, 'אל תטמאו בכל אלה,' where one sin alone clearly makes a person impure.

steps.title: Here too, one trait is enough
steps.stepSummary: Just like the טומאה פסוק, 'עושה אלה' means doing even one of these traits.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it means with any one of all these.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים apply the proof back to תהלים: doing even one of these traits earns the promise 'he will never fall.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison is now complete. The same reading that is clear in ויקרא is applied to תהלים, which answers רבן גמליאל's worry.

keyTerms.meaning: With any one of all these

steps.whatToRemember: רבן גמליאל feared you need all eleven traits. The חכמים showed from the wording, and from 'אל תטמאו בכל אלה,' that even one trait brings the promise 'לא ימוט לעולם.'
steps.whyThisMatters: It is a comforting message: a person doesn't have to be perfect in every trait to earn this blessing; real excellence in even one counts.

phrases.english: Here too, it means with any one of all these.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא נָמֵי בְּאַחַת מִכׇּל אֵלּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the proof from step 17 back to the פסוק in תהלים.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Doing even one of the traits of תהלים 15 earns the promise 'עושה אלה לא ימוט לעולם.'

steps.title: ישעיהו narrows the מצוות down to six traits
steps.stepSummary: ישעיהו takes the תרי"ג מצוות and sums them up in six traits, based on a פסוק in ישעיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: ישעיהו came and summed them up in six, as it says: 'He who walks righteously, and speaks uprightly; he who hates money gained by cheating, who shakes his hands so they hold no bribe, who closes his ears from hearing about bloodshed, and shuts his eyes from looking at evil.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues רבי שמלאי's list. After דוד's eleven traits, it now shows ישעיהו using just six traits to sum up all the מצוות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern is that each later נביא packs the 613 מצוות into fewer and fewer core traits. Here ישעיהו's פסוק lists six behaviors. The next steps will explain what each trait means.

keyTerms.meaning: He 'stood them up on' or based them on (summed them up in)

phrases.english: Isaiah came and established them upon six,
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the 613 מצוות from the start of רבי שמלאי's teaching.

phrases.english: as it is written: "He who walks righteously, and speaks uprightly;
he who despises the gain of oppressions,
who shakes his hands from holding bribes,
who stops his ears from hearing of blood,
and shuts his eyes from looking upon evil."

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּא יְשַׁעְיָהוּ וְהֶעֱמִידָן עַל שֵׁשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from דוד's eleven traits to the next stage in רבי שמלאי's list: ישעיהו's six.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ישעיהו summed up all the מצוות in six traits listed in ישעיהו 33:15.

steps.title: Walking righteously is like אברהם
steps.stepSummary: The first trait, 'walking righteously,' describes someone like אברהם אבינו, as a פסוק about him shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He who walks righteously' is אברהם אבינו, as it says about him: 'For I know him, that he will command his children... to do righteousness and justice.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts explaining ישעיהו's six traits one by one. The first trait is linked to אברהם אבינו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא proves the link with a פסוק about אברהם, where ה׳ says אברהם will teach his family to do צדקה. Since that פסוק uses the same idea of righteousness, 'walking righteously' points to living the way אברהם did.

keyTerms.meaning: I have known him (I hold him close)

phrases.english: "He who walks righteously" — this is our forefather Abraham,

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב ״כִּי יְדַעְתִּיו לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: as it is written: "For I have known him, so that he will command, etc."
phrases.notes: בראשית 18:19. The rest of the פסוק talks about doing צדקה and justice, which is the link.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֹלֵךְ צְדָקוֹת זֶה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins explaining the six traits listed in step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'הולך צדקות' describes someone who lives like אברהם אבינו.

steps.title: Speaking uprightly means not shaming others in public
steps.stepSummary: The second trait, 'speaking uprightly,' means never embarrassing another person in front of others.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And speaks uprightly' is someone who does not shame his friend in public.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second trait. 'Speaking uprightly' is about how you talk to other people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not read 'upright speech' only as telling the truth. It defines it as speech that protects another person's dignity, especially in front of a crowd.

keyTerms.meaning: In public, in front of many people

phrases.english: "And speaks uprightly" —

phrases.aramaic: זֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַקְנִיט פְּנֵי חֲבֵירוֹ בָּרַבִּים.
phrases.english: this is one who does not shame his fellow in public.
phrases.notes: Literally 'does not upset his friend's face,' meaning he doesn't make him blush with shame.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדֹבֵר מֵישָׁרִים זֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַקְנִיט פְּנֵי חֲבֵירוֹ בָּרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list, explaining the second of the six traits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'דובר מישרים' is someone who does not embarrass others in public.

steps.title: Despising dishonest gain, like רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע
steps.stepSummary: The third trait, 'despising the gain of oppressions,' is shown by the example of רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He who hates money gained by cheating' is someone like רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third trait by pointing to a real person who lived it: רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of defining the trait in words, the גמרא gives a model person. This matches the way the earlier traits of דוד were also illustrated by specific sages, like רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי in step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: Gain that comes from cheating or oppressing others

phrases.english: "He who despises the gain of oppressions" —
such as Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֹאֵס בְּבֶצַע מַעֲשַׁקּוֹת כְּגוֹן רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אֱלִישָׁע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list, explaining the third of the six traits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'מואס בבצע מעשקות' is illustrated by רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע.

steps.title: Fourth trait: shaking off bribes
steps.stepSummary: The fourth trait, 'shaking his hands from holding bribes,' is shown by the example of רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Who shakes his hands from holding a bribe' means someone like רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the fourth trait in the פסוק and gives a real person as the example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the earlier traits, the גמרא doesn't define this one in abstract terms. It points to a well-known sage who lived it. That sage stood out for staying far away from anything that even looked like a bribe.

keyTerms.meaning: Shakes off his hands, refusing to hold something

phrases.english: "Who shakes his hands from holding a bribe"
such as Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֹעֵר כַּפָּיו מִתְּמֹךְ בַּשֹּׁחַד כְּגוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of six traits with the fourth one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Shaking off bribes describes someone like רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי.

steps.title: Fifth trait: not staying silent when a scholar is insulted
steps.stepSummary: 'Stopping his ears from hearing blood' means not hearing a תלמיד חכם insulted and keeping quiet, as רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון did.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Who stops his ears from hearing blood' means someone who will not hear a Torah scholar being insulted and stay silent, such as רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the fifth trait and gives an example sage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'hearing blood' are not about murder here. The גמרא reads them as hearing a צורבא מרבנן being put down. The trait is to refuse to let that pass in silence.

keyTerms.meaning: A young Torah scholar, a תלמיד חכם

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as 'he plugs his ears and ignores it.' The point is the opposite: he does not hear the insult and stay quiet. He speaks up.

phrases.english: "Who stops his ear from hearing blood"
one who does not hear the insult of a Torah scholar

phrases.aramaic: וְשָׁתֵיק, כְּגוֹן רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן.
phrases.english: and remain silent, such as Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֹטֵם אׇזְנוֹ מִשְּׁמֹעַ דָּמִים דְּלָא שָׁמַע בְּזִילוּתָא דְּצוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list with the fifth trait.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stopping the ears from 'blood' means refusing to stay silent when a תלמיד חכם is insulted.

steps.title: Sixth trait: shutting the eyes from evil
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא explains 'shutting his eyes from seeing evil' as not looking at women while they stand over the laundry.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And shuts his eyes from seeing evil' follows רבי חייא בר אבא, who said: this is someone who does not look at women when they are standing over the laundry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the sixth and last trait using a statement of רבי חייא בר אבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the example is not a person but a situation. 'Seeing evil' is a real, everyday temptation: looking at women while they wash clothes. The trait is guarding your eyes in just that kind of moment.

phrases.english: "And shuts his eyes from seeing evil"
follows Rabbi Chiya bar Abba,
for Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said:
This is one who does not look at women
when they are standing over the laundry.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעֹצֵם עֵינָיו מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע כְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the list with the sixth trait.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Shutting the eyes from evil means not looking at women while they do laundry.

steps.title: The reward: he will dwell on high
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא closes the six traits with the next פסוק, which promises that such a person 'will dwell on high.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'He will dwell on high.'
steps.whatsHappening: After listing all six traits, the גמרא quotes the next פסוק in ישעיהו to show the reward for someone who lives by them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ties the whole list together. ישעיהו didn't only list six traits that sum up the מצוות; he also promised a reward. Whoever lives this way will be raised up and protected.
steps.whatToRemember: ישעיהו sums up the תרי"ג מצוות in six traits: walking righteously (like אברהם), speaking uprightly (never embarrassing others in public), despising unfair gain, shaking off bribes, refusing to stay silent when a scholar is insulted, and guarding one's eyes. The one who has them 'will dwell on high.'

phrases.english: And it is written: "He will dwell on high."

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְתִיב הוּא מְרוֹמִים יִשְׁכּוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Wraps up the six-trait list by quoting the promised reward from the next פסוק.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Someone who lives by ישעיהו's six traits is promised that he will dwell on high.

steps.title: מיכה sums up the מצוות in three
steps.stepSummary: מיכה boiled all the מצוות down to three principles: doing justice, loving kindness, and walking modestly with ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: מיכה came and built all the מצוות on three things, as the פסוק says: 'Man, you have been told what is good and what ה׳ asks of you: only to do justice, love kindness, and walk modestly with your God.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps counting down. After the earlier נביאים, now מיכה sums up all the מצוות in just three principles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each נביא picks fewer principles that still contain the whole Torah. מיכה's three come straight from one פסוק. The next step will explain what each of the three means.

keyTerms.meaning: He 'stood them up' on, meaning he based all the מצוות on these principles

phrases.english: Micah came and established them upon three,
as it is written: "It has been told to you, O man, what is good,
and what does the Lord require of you
only to do justice
and to love kindness
and to walk modestly with your God."
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּא מִיכָה וְהֶעֱמִידָן עַל שָׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the countdown of נביאים summing up the מצוות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מיכה based all the מצוות on three principles: justice, kindness, and walking modestly with ה׳.

steps.title: Explaining מיכה's three principles
steps.stepSummary: Justice means fair judgment. Loving kindness means גמילות חסדים. Walking modestly means burying the dead and bringing a bride to her wedding.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'To do justice' means judgment. 'Love kindness' means acts of kindness. 'Walk modestly' means taking the dead out for burial and bringing a bride to her wedding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains each of the three phrases in מיכה's פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first two are fairly direct. The surprise is the third: 'walking modestly' is applied to funerals and weddings, which are public events. That surprise sets up the קל וחומר in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Taking the dead out for burial
Bringing a bride to her wedding

phrases.english: "To do justice": this is judgment.
"To love kindness": this is acts of kindness.
"And to walk modestly": this is taking out the dead for burial
and bringing in a bride to her wedding.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט זֶה הַדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the three phrases of the פסוק quoted in step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Walking modestly is applied to burying the dead and bringing a bride to her wedding.

steps.title: A קל וחומר for doing private מצוות quietly
steps.stepSummary: If the Torah asks for modesty even with public events like funerals and weddings, then מצוות that are usually done privately must surely be done quietly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this a קל וחומר? If for things that are not usually done privately the Torah says 'walk modestly,' then for things usually done privately, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a lesson from the last explanation using a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Funerals and weddings are naturally public, yet the פסוק still asks for modesty. So things that are naturally private, like giving צדקה, should certainly be done quietly and not shown off.

keyTerms.meaning: Reasoning from a lighter case to a stronger one

steps.whatToRemember: Even public מצוות call for modesty, so private מצוות surely should not be shown off.

phrases.english: And is this not a קל וחומר?

phrases.aramaic: וּמָה דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין דַּרְכָּן לַעֲשׂוֹתָן בְּצִנְעָא,
phrases.english: If for things that are not usually done privately,
phrases.notes: He means funerals and weddings from the line before.

phrases.english: the Torah said "walk modestly,"
then things that are usually done privately,
all the more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: וַהֲלֹא דְּבָרִים קַל וָחוֹמֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a קל וחומר from the explanation of 'walk modestly' in step 28.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Private מצוות must surely be done quietly.

steps.title: ישעיהו sums up the מצוות in two
steps.stepSummary: ישעיהו based all the מצוות on two principles: keeping justice and doing righteousness.
steps.simpleTranslation: ישעיהו came again and built them on two, as it says: 'So says ה׳: Keep justice and do righteousness.'
steps.whatsHappening: The countdown continues. ישעיהו now sums up all the מצוות in two principles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list shrinks from three to two. The word חזר ('again') hints that ישעיהו already appeared earlier in the countdown, and now he narrows it even more.

phrases.english: Isaiah came back and established them upon two,
as it is stated: "So says the Lord:
Keep justice and do righteousness."

steps.triggerLanguage: חָזַר יְשַׁעְיָהוּ וְהֶעֱמִידָן עַל שְׁתַּיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the countdown from three to two.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ישעיהו based all the מצוות on justice and righteousness.

steps.title: עמוס sums up the מצוות in one
steps.stepSummary: עמוס seems to base all the מצוות on one principle: 'Seek Me and live.'
steps.simpleTranslation: עמוס came and built them on one, as it says: 'So says ה׳ to the house of Israel: Seek Me and live.'
steps.whatsHappening: The countdown reaches one. עמוס seems to put the whole Torah into a single idea: seek ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the first attempt to find one single principle. The next step will question whether this פסוק really counts as one principle.

phrases.english: Amos came and established them upon one,
as it is stated: "So says the Lord to the house of Israel:
Seek Me and live."

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּא עָמוֹס וְהֶעֱמִידָן עַל אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the countdown from two to one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עמוס based all the מצוות on 'Seek Me and live.'

steps.title: Maybe 'seek Me' means through the whole Torah
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק argues that 'Seek Me' could mean seek ה׳ through every מצוה, so it is not one principle.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק challenged: Say it means 'seek Me through the whole Torah!'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק challenges the idea that עמוס reduced everything to one principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק does not say how to seek ה׳. It could mean 'seek Me by keeping all the מצוות,' which brings back all 613 instead of reducing them to one.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק:
phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges this:
Say it means: seek Me through the whole Torah!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof from עמוס in step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that עמוס based all the מצוות on one principle.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Seek Me' is open-ended and could mean seek ה׳ through all the מצוות, so it is not a single principle.

steps.title: חבקוק is the one who sums it up in one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא switches: חבקוק is the one who based all the מצוות on one principle, 'The righteous person lives by his faith.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: חבקוק came and built them on one, as it says: 'The righteous person shall live by his faith.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the challenge and replaces עמוס with חבקוק as the one who reduced everything to a single principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חבקוק's פסוק clearly names one thing, אמונה, so it cannot be read as 'all the מצוות.' This ends the countdown with faith as the root of the whole Torah.
steps.whatToRemember: The final single principle that holds up the whole Torah is faith, from חבקוק.
steps.confusionAlert: עמוס is not the final answer. After רב נחמן בר יצחק's challenge, the גמרא replaces him with חבקוק.

phrases.english: Rather: Habakkuk came
and established them upon one,
as it is stated: "But the righteous person shall live by his faith."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בָּא חֲבַקּוּק וְהֶעֱמִידָן עַל אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 32 by replacing עמוס with חבקוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the source with a clearer one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: עמוס's 'Seek Me and live' was the single principle.
steps.terutzMaskana: חבקוק's 'The righteous shall live by his faith' is the single principle.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All the מצוות rest on faith.

steps.title: Four decrees of משה cancelled by four נביאים
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא teaches that משה made four harsh decrees on Israel, and four נביאים later cancelled them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: משה רבינו made four decrees on Israel, and four נביאים came and cancelled them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. רבי יוסי בר חנינא gives a general statement that the next lines will spell out one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a heading. The point is that later נביאים softened harsh statements of משה. Each decree and the נביא who cancelled it will now be listed.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina says:

phrases.aramaic: אַרְבַּע גְּזֵירוֹת גָּזַר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל,
phrases.english: Moses our teacher issued four decrees upon Israel,
four prophets came and cancelled them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא אַרְבַּע גְּזֵירוֹת גָּזַר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new aggadic teaching after the countdown ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Four of משה's harsh decrees were cancelled by four later נביאים.

steps.title: First decree: safety only on יעקב's level, cancelled by עמוס
steps.stepSummary: משה said Israel will be safe 'like יעקב,' meaning only at a very high level. עמוס prayed 'How can יעקב stand?' and ה׳ relented.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said: 'Israel dwells safely, alone, like יעקב.' עמוס came and cancelled it, as it says: 'Stop, please, how can יעקב stand?' and it says: 'ה׳ relented about this.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first of the four decrees and shows how עמוס cancelled it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה's words imply Israel is safe only when they are as great as יעקב, which is very hard. עמוס pleaded that יעקב is small and cannot stand that test, and ה׳ agreed, so the condition was softened.

keyTerms.meaning: The 'fountain' of יעקב, read as 'like יעקב'

phrases.english: Moses said:
"And Israel dwells in safety, alone,
the fountain of Jacob,"
Amos came and cancelled it,
as it is stated: "Cease, please; how shall Jacob stand, etc."
phrases.notes: עמוס 7:5. The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and it is written: "The Lord relented about this."

steps.triggerLanguage: מֹשֶׁה אָמַר וַיִּשְׁכֹּן יִשְׂרָאֵל בֶּטַח בָּדָד עֵין יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first example of the four decrees announced in step 34.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה's condition that Israel is safe only on יעקב's level was cancelled through עמוס's prayer.

steps.title: Second decree: no rest among the nations, softened by ירמיה
steps.stepSummary: משה said Israel would have no rest in exile. ירמיה later said ה׳ will bring Israel rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said: 'Among those nations you will have no rest.' ירמיה came and said: 'Going to give rest to Israel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the list of four decrees from step 34. This is the second one: משה said Israel would have no rest in exile, and ירמיה answered that ה׳ would give them rest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each entry follows the same pattern: a harsh פסוק from משה, then a נביא with a softer message. Here 'no rest' becomes 'I will give rest,' even while Israel is in exile.

keyTerms.meaning: you will find rest or calm
a decree, a harsh statement of what will happen

phrases.english: Moses said: "And among those nations you shall have no rest,"
Jeremiah came and said:
"Going to give rest to Israel."

steps.triggerLanguage: מֹשֶׁה אָמַר: ״וּבַגּוֹיִם הָהֵם לֹא תַרְגִּיעַ״, בָּא יִרְמְיָה וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second item in the list of four decrees begun in step 34; step 35 was the first.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה's 'no rest in exile' was softened by ירמיה's promise of rest.

steps.title: Third decree: children punished for parents' sins, cancelled by יחזקאל
steps.stepSummary: משה said ה׳ punishes children for the sins of their fathers. יחזקאל cancelled it: only the sinner dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said: 'He punishes the sin of fathers upon the children.' יחזקאל came and cancelled it: 'The soul that sins, it alone shall die.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the third decree. משה said children can be punished for their parents' sins, and יחזקאל taught that each person is punished only for their own sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: As with עמוס in step 35, the גמרא says the נביא 'cancelled it' (ביטלה). The harsh idea of punishing children is replaced by personal responsibility: the one who sins is the one who is punished.

keyTerms.meaning: punishes the sin of fathers upon the children

phrases.aramaic: מֹשֶׁה אָמַר: ״פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים״,
phrases.english: Moses said: "He visits the sin of the fathers upon the children,"
Ezekiel came and cancelled it:
"The soul that sins, it shall die."

steps.triggerLanguage: מֹשֶׁה אָמַר: ״פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים״, בָּא יְחֶזְקֵאל וּבִיטְּלָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third item in the same list of four decrees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה's 'children punished for fathers' sins' was cancelled by יחזקאל's 'only the sinner dies.'

steps.title: Fourth decree: lost among the nations, softened by ישעיהו
steps.stepSummary: משה said Israel will be lost among the nations. ישעיהו said a great שופר will gather the lost ones back.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said: 'You will be lost among the nations.' ישעיהו came and said: 'On that day a great שופר will be blown,' and the lost ones will return.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the fourth and last decree. משה warned that Israel would be lost in exile, and ישעיהו promised that a great שופר will bring them back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Lost' sounds final, but ישעיהו's פסוק goes on to talk about 'those lost in the land of Assyria' coming back. So the lostness is not permanent. This finishes the list of four from step 34.

keyTerms.meaning: a great שופר, the signal of the final return from exile

steps.whatToRemember: The four decrees of משה and the נביאים who softened them: 'like יעקב' (עמוס), 'no rest' (ירמיה), 'sins of the fathers' (יחזקאל), 'lost among the nations' (ישעיהו).

phrases.english: Moses said: "And you shall be lost among the nations,"
Isaiah came and said:
"And it shall be on that day, a great shofar shall be sounded."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 27:13. The פסוק continues: 'and those lost in the land of Assyria shall come.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מֹשֶׁה אָמַר ״וַאֲבַדְתֶּם בַּגּוֹיִם״, בָּא יְשַׁעְיָהוּ וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fourth and final item, completing the list of four decrees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה's 'lost among the nations' was softened by ישעיהו's great שופר of return.

steps.title: רב is afraid of the verse 'You shall be lost among the nations'
steps.stepSummary: רב says he is afraid of the פסוק 'וַאֲבַדְתֶּם בַּגּוֹיִם.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: I am afraid of this פסוק: 'And you shall be lost among the nations.'
steps.whatsHappening: Picking up on the last decree, רב says this פסוק scares him. This sets up a back-and-forth about whether the פסוק is really as frightening as it sounds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though ישעיהו softened it, רב still feels the word 'lost' could mean Israel disappears completely. The next steps test whether that fear is justified.

phrases.english: Rav said: I am afraid of this verse:
"And you shall be lost among the nations."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: מִסְתְּפֵינָא מֵהַאי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the fourth decree just quoted, opening a discussion of how scary that פסוק is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב fears that 'lost among the nations' means permanent loss.

steps.title: רב פפא: 'lost' can mean a lost item that is searched for
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא challenges רב: 'lost' can mean like a lost object that its owner looks for, which is a hopeful meaning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא challenged this: Maybe it means like a lost object that is being searched for, as it says: 'I have strayed like a lost lamb; seek Your servant.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא pushes back on רב's fear. He says 'lost' can mean something its owner is still looking for, and brings a פסוק that uses the word that way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is on רב's reading of the word 'lost.' A lost lamb is not gone forever; its owner goes looking for it. So the פסוק may hint that ה׳ will search for Israel and bring them back.

keyTerms.meaning: challenges it, raises a strong objection
a lost object that is being searched for

phrases.english: Rav Pappa challenged this:
Perhaps it means like a lost item that is searched for,
as it is written: "I have gone astray like a lost lamb;
seek Your servant"!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב פָּפָּא: דִּלְמָא כַּאֲבֵידָה הַמִּתְבַּקֶּשֶׁת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly challenges רב's fear in step 39.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'lost' is used elsewhere for something its owner seeks, like the lost lamb in תהלים, so it need not mean permanent loss.

steps.title: Rather, רב feared the end of the verse: 'Your enemies' land will consume you'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shifts: רב's fear was really from the end of that פסוק, 'and the land of your enemies shall consume you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב was afraid because of the end of the פסוק: 'And the land of your enemies shall consume you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts רב פפא's point about the word 'lost.' It explains that what scared רב was the second half of the same פסוק, which talks about being 'consumed.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Lost' can be hopeful, but 'consumed' sounds like being destroyed completely. So the source of רב's fear moves from the beginning of the פסוק to its end.

keyTerms.meaning: rather, a sign that the גמרא is switching to a new explanation
the end part of a text

phrases.english: Rather, it was from the end of the verse,
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is the corrected wording, making clear it's the end of the same פסוק.

phrases.english: "And the land of your enemies shall consume you."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִסֵּיפָא דִּקְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's challenge by moving רב's fear to a different part of the פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Relocating the source: same fear, different words in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב feared the word 'lost' at the start of the פסוק.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב feared the word 'consume' at the end of the פסוק.

steps.title: מר זוטרא: 'consumed' like cucumbers and gourds, not completely
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא challenges this too: 'consume' may mean like eating cucumbers and gourds, where some is always left.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא challenged this: Maybe it means like eating cucumbers and gourds, which are not eaten completely.
steps.whatsHappening: מר זוטרא pushes back on the new reading. He says 'consume' can mean partly eaten, like cucumbers and gourds, so even this part of the פסוק has a hopeful side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With cucumbers and gourds, part is left over, and new plants can grow from what remains. So 'consume' does not have to mean total destruction. Both halves of the פסוק can now be read hopefully.
steps.whatToRemember: רב feared 'וַאֲבַדְתֶּם בַּגּוֹיִם,' but each scary word gets a hopeful reading. 'Lost' is like a lamb its owner searches for (רב פפא), and 'consumed' is like cucumbers and gourds, where something always remains (מר זוטרא).

phrases.english: Mar Zutra challenged this:
Perhaps it means like the eating of cucumbers and gourds.
phrases.notes: These are never eaten completely; some is left over, and more can grow from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ מָר זוּטְרָא: דִּלְמָא כַּאֲכִילַת קִישּׁוּאִין וְדִילּוּעִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new explanation of רב's fear given in step 41.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'וְאָכְלָה אֶתְכֶם' means complete destruction
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Eating' can describe partial eating, like cucumbers and gourds where some remains, so the פסוק need not mean total loss.

steps.title: Four sages hear the noise of Rome: three cry and one laughs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a story: רבן גמליאל, רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, רבי יהושע, and רבי עקיבא hear the crowds of רומי from 120 מיל away. The others start crying, but רבי עקיבא laughs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once, רבן גמליאל, רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, רבי יהושע, and רבי עקיבא were walking on the road. They heard the noise of the crowds of רומי from Puteoli, 120 מיל away. The others began to cry, and רבי עקיבא was laughing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a new story that sets up a puzzle: why would רבי עקיבא laugh when everyone else is crying?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story continues the theme of the last few steps: being lost among the nations and the hope of return. The noise of רומי heard from so far away shows how huge and powerful the enemy city is. The opposite reactions (crying versus laughing) set up the question-and-answer that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: And it once happened (opening of a story)
Its crowds / the noise of its many people
A unit of distance, roughly a kilometer
Rome, the capital of the empire that destroyed the בית המקדש

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known story about how to look at the suffering of exile. It sets up רבי עקיבא's famous hopeful lesson, which comes on the next amud.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְבָר הָיָה רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה
phrases.english: And it once was that Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
and Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
were walking on the road,
and they heard the sound of the crowds of Rome
from Puteoli, at a distance of one hundred and twenty mil,
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets, 'at a distance,' is the corrected wording.

phrases.english: and they began weeping,
phrases.notes: 'They' means the other three חכמים, not רבי עקיבא.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Akiva was laughing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְבָר הָיָה רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the back-and-forth about רב's fear of exile, the גמרא brings a story about sages facing the reality of exile.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story is set up: the sight of רומי's power makes three חכמים cry while רבי עקיבא laughs.

steps.title: The sages ask רבי עקיבא why he is laughing
steps.stepSummary: The other חכמים ask רבי עקיבא what reason he has to laugh.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Why are you laughing?
steps.whatsHappening: The other חכמים ask the obvious question: how can רבי עקיבא laugh at a moment like this?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their question shows that laughing seems completely out of place. The reader is meant to feel the same surprise and wait for רבי עקיבא's explanation.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: מִפְּנֵי מָה אַתָּה מְשַׂחֵק?
phrases.english: They said to him: For what reason are you laughing?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: מִפְּנֵי מָה אַתָּה מְשַׂחֵק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the strange reaction described in step 43.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי עקיבא is laughing when the others are crying.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא asks them first why they are crying
steps.stepSummary: Instead of answering, רבי עקיבא turns the question around and asks why they are crying.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: And you, why are you crying?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא does not answer yet; he asks them to explain their crying first. This sets up the next move, where they explain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By hearing their reason first, רבי עקיבא can answer them using the very same facts that made them cry. His answer will make more sense once their worry is spelled out.

phrases.english: He said to them:
And you, for what reason are you weeping?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם: וְאַתֶּם מִפְּנֵי מָה אַתֶּם בּוֹכִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to their question with a question of his own.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the other חכמים are crying.

steps.title: The sages explain: idol worshippers live in peace while our Temple is burned
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים explain their tears: the nations who worship idols live safe and calm, while the בית המקדש, the footstool of our God, has been burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: These nations bow to idols and burn incense to false gods, yet they live safely and calmly. And for us, the בית המקדש, the footstool of our God, is burned.
steps.whatsHappening: The other חכמים answer רבי עקיבא's question: they are crying because of the painful contrast between רומי's peace and the destroyed בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their complaint is about how unfair things look: people who serve idols are rewarded with safety, while the place where ה׳'s presence rested is in ruins. The sentence is not finished here; it continues on the next amud, where רבי עקיבא gives his answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Burning incense (as an act of worship)
The house of the footstool of our God: the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence breaks off at 'is burned.' Their complaint continues on the next amud, and רבי עקיבא's reason for laughing comes there.

phrases.english: They said to him: These gentiles,
who bow to false gods
and burn incense to idols,
dwell securely and tranquilly,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָנוּ, בֵּית הֲדוֹם רַגְלֵי אֱלֹהֵינוּ שָׂרוּף
phrases.english: and for us, the House of the footstool of our God is burnt
phrases.notes: A poetic name for the בית המקדש, as if it is where ה׳'s 'feet rest' in this world.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: הַלָּלוּ גּוֹיִם שֶׁמִּשְׁתַּחֲוִים לַעֲצַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי עקיבא's counter-question from step 45.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They cry because idol worshippers live in peace while the בית המקדש lies burned.
